articles.title: Sandpapergate: Usman Khawaja and David Warner question Cricket Australia’s new forum following explosive fallout
articles.summary: Cricket Australia: "After careful consideration, the CA Board has decided to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and perspectives"; forum set up following explosive claims in Usman Khawaja's book
articles.body:
Debate about the ball tampering drama of 2018 has been raging Down Under since the publication of explosive claims in Khawaja's autobiography.

Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft suffered lengthy bans eight years ago after a short investigation found them to be solely guilty, but Khawaja has alleged the entire squad and staff were aware of the plot.

Warner and reserve seamer Chadd Sayers have backed his account, while current Australia captain Pat Cummins has issued a comprehensive denial.

But Cricket Australia (CA) has already ruled out the prospect of any new punishments and has instead invited all parties to share their recollections - without fear of reprisals.

The reaction of two of ​the main protagonists to the announcement was not entirely positive, with both Warner and Khawaja expressing reservations about whose version of ​events would emerge.

"I appreciate where their heart is, and I'll support the board in this. I just wanted to take accountability, and ⁠I've done it for the three guys who I think were unfairly treated," Khawaja told Fox Sports .

"I could go in there and say something, but then the board can decide that they're not going to release that, and I just feel like then we just go in a circle again."

Warner, sat with Khawaja on ⁠a punditry panel for Wednesday's ODI between Australia and England, echoed his former opening partner's comments.

"I would ​have liked an open, independent inquiry, and the people that were there at the time actually can come forward and speak, because ​we have no idea about what's happened behind closed doors," he said.

"Look, we put our hands up. We accepted what Cricket ‌Australia handed down to us. It's not about penalties. ​It's just about coming up with transparency and accountability."

Darren Lehmann, Australia's head coach in 2018, was more positive.

"I think we've done the best of a terrible situation. For me, it's the light at the end of the tunnel."

CA chief explains new Sandpapergate forum

CA chief executive Todd Greenberg and interim chair David Boon appeared at a hastily convened press conference in Hobart to announce a move they hope will take the heat out of the controversy.

"After careful consideration, the CA Board has decided to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and perspectives," said Boon.

"We believe this is in the best interests of the game. For almost a decade, the fallout from those events has remained part of the conversation around Australian cricket.

"It has been a difficult chapter for many people and, increasingly, the ongoing debate has become a distraction from the game. We believe it is time for a circuit breaker.

"This forum is not about relitigating the past. It is about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful environment, and for our sport to listen.

"Australian cricket is at its strongest when it is united. We owe it to everyone who loves the game to make every reasonable effort to move forward together, with understanding, respect and perspective."

Healy: Rehashing Sandpapergate a massive stain on cricket

Also on Wednesday, Australian Test great Ian Healy questioned why Khawaja had reignited the debate with the release of his book eight years after the fact.

Healy claimed Australian cricketers on the sandpaper tour will now be remembered as "liars forever" following the claims.

"Hopefully we got close to the truth in the investigation; those who didn't get an interview and didn't go forward, they're guilty whistleblowers now," Healy said on SEN radio .

"They didn't come forward when it was saveable, now there's a massive stain on cricket and they'll be known as liars forever.

"There is no reason this should have been rehashed. This was not Uzzy's story to tell, he wasn't involved and didn't do anything. Why write about that? He should have done it the day after the occurrence. It's Davey's book to write."

articles.title: No Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, no problem! Bihar pull off thrilling two-wicket win over Delhi in Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bihar showed they can win without their star batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, pulling off a thrilling two-wicket victory over Delhi in the Syed
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bihar showed they can win without their star batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, pulling off a thrilling two-wicket victory over Delhi in the Syed Mushtaq Ali Trophy at the Daly College Ground in Indore.Chasing a massive target of 225, Bihar reached 227 for eight in 19.5 overs, with Mayank Kumar and Prashant Singh holding their nerve in the final overs to take the team across the line.Sooryavanshi was missing from the Bihar side as he is set to join the India A squad for the ACC Men's Asia Cup Rising Stars 2026, which begins in Doha on November 20. India A will open their campaign against Nepal.Yash Dhull's century powers Delhi to 224After being asked to bat, Delhi posted a huge total of 224 for five in their 20 overs, thanks to a brilliant century from Yash Dhull.Dhull smashed 125 off just 59 balls, hitting 16 fours and seven sixes. He dominated the innings and shared a 126-run partnership with Tejasvi Dahiya, who scored 51 off 25 balls.Dahiya struck four fours and four sixes as Delhi finished with a run rate of 11.2.Raghuvendra Pratap Singh was Bihar's most successful bowler, picking up three wickets for 44 runs. Prashant Singh and Suraj Kashyap took one wicket each.Loharuka, Bipin give Bihar a flying startBihar began their chase aggressively, scoring 96 runs in the first six overs.Wicketkeeper-batter Ayush Loharuka led the charge with a quick 50 off 22 balls, including seven fours and three sixes. He added 103 runs with Bipin Saurabh for the second wicket.Bipin also played an attacking knock, scoring 49 off just 19 balls with three fours and five sixes. Their partnership put Bihar in a strong position in the chase.However, Delhi fought back through their spinners. Digvesh Singh Rathi picked up three wickets for 47 runs, while Suyash Sharma and Keshav Dabas claimed one wicket each.Mayank, Prashant keep their nerve in tense finishBihar lost wickets at regular intervals after the strong start and slipped to 189 for eight in the 17th over. With 36 runs still needed from the final three overs, the match was in the balance.Mayank Kumar and Prashant Singh then turned the game around with an important unbeaten partnership.Mayank provided the late fireworks, hitting three sixes in his unbeaten 24 off 13 balls. Prashant remained not out on 13 off eight deliveries, hitting two fours.The pair took 19 runs off the 18th over bowled by Keshav Dabas, including two sixes from Mayank. They then collected five runs in the 19th over before Prashant struck a boundary off Nitish Rana in the final over to seal the win with one ball remaining.Bihar finished on 227 for eight in 19.5 overs to register a memorable two-wicket victory.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: India and the tail: The old habit needs to die now
articles.summary: Wellington: India have struggled to wrap up opposition innings over the years, and the problem has persisted since Shubman Gill took over as captain ahead
articles.body: Wellington: India have struggled to wrap up opposition innings over the years, and the problem has persisted since Shubman Gill took over as captain ahead of the England tour last year. In the 12 Tests played under his leadership, opposition lower-order batters have repeatedly frustrated India, scoring crucial runs from No. 8 onwards.England's lower order added 369 runs in eight innings, the West Indies scored 201 in four, while South Africa accumulated 213 in just three.The most frustrating runs came during the recent away series against Sri Lanka, where India conceded 145 runs in four innings and saw the opposition tail survive for 95.2 overs. This played a major role in India missing out on crucial World Test Championship (WTC) points, as the Colombo Test ended in a draw.In the upcoming Test series against New Zealand, India need to be wary of the lower-order threat, as the hosts have bowlers who are more than handy with the bat. In lively conditions, 30-40 extra runs can significantly affect the contest. This was evident in the fifth ODI, when Mohammed Siraj and Arshdeep Singh's useful contributions at Nos. 10 and 11 proved decisive.Bowling coach Morne Morkel acknowledged that this is a "very important" area, as New Zealand have bowlers capable of putting together small, but very crucial, partnerships."Very important. At the end of the day, to win a Test match, you need to bowl the team out. Like I said, we always respect and do a lot of work with lower-order batters. Gone are the days when you can just start the heavy roller and get those right, because those crucial sort of partnerships we do see happen more often," Morkel told reporters in Wellington."If you look at the New Zealand lower order, they're all guys who are capable of getting small-level partnerships. I think for us it's going to be crucial that we understand that, acknowledge that, and still do the things that help us get the wickets, sort of bowling the top order out," Morkel said.I think at times we can get a little bit greedy, get carried away, and then before you know it, there's a 20- or 30-run partnership, or guys find a little bit of comfort at the crease.During the Sri Lanka series, India were tactically exposed because there were passages of play when they never looked to dismiss the set batters. Open fields became common, allowing the tailenders to buy time and grow in confidence as the innings and partnerships progressed. Morkel felt that not being "a little bit greedy" would be important, and said they had plans to prevent the tail from wagging."I think at times we can get a little bit greedy, get carried away, and then before you know it, there's a 20- or 30-run partnership, or guys find a little bit of comfort at the crease. So how we can attack that better, can we be more aggressive maybe with a short ball, a field setting, but still, a good ball is a good ball on any wicket, and can we test the defence of a tailender more consistently from both ends," Morkel explained.The former South African fast bowler, who has experience playing in these conditions and was particularly effective at cleaning up the lower order, called for a more proactive approach from both ends."I think at times we were maybe a little bit, a little bit sort of missing our mark from both ends in terms of knocking the tail over, in terms of bowling combinations at the time, expecting it will happen and not actually committing to it," Morkel said.Gill has repeatedly spoken about how quickly momentum can shift because of frustrating lower-order contributions. He has regularly called for his bowlers to contribute in this regard and will now need to be on top of his tactical game to ensure opposition lower-order batters do not run away with the momentum.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Scotland coast to win over Ireland as both reach Super Six phase
articles.summary: Scotland's bowlers make short work of Ireland in a comfortable eight-wicket victory as both teams progress to the Super Six stage at the Women's Emerging Nations Trophy in Dubai.
articles.body:
Ireland 71 (19.3 overs): Lewis 20; Gordon 4-4, Maqsood 3-15

Scotland 72-2 (8.3 overs): Carter 30, Fraser 21

Scotland's bowlers made short work of Ireland in a comfortable eight-wicket victory as both teams progressed to the Super Six stage at the Women's Emerging Nations Trophy in Dubai.

Kirstie Gordon ripped through the Irish top order, the left-arm spinner taking four wickets for just four runs.

Abtaha Maqsood claimed three wickets, Kathryn Bryce struck twice and Priyanaz Chatterji picked up her 50th T20 International wicket as Ireland were dismissed for just 71.

Captain Gaby Lewis top scored for Ireland on 20, with Georgina Dempsey (12), Abbi Harrison (11) and Jane Maguire (11*) the others to reach double figures.

In reply, Darcey Carter (30) and Katherine Fraser (21) enjoyed a 53-run opening partnership, with Kathryn Bryce (7*) and Sarah Bryce (4*) steering Scotland home in the ninth over.

Scotland finished second behind unbeaten Sri Lanka in Group A, with Ireland in third place.

Netherlands and Pakistan are guaranteed passage from Group B as Zimbabwe and Bangladesh vie for the remaining spot.

"I was trying to use the surface as much as I could, and try force them to take the difficult options and I'm glad the skipper kept me on in the powerplay, when you know they're coming out well you want to stay on," said player of the match Kirstie Gordon.

"I think length was key, that's something we've spoken about throughout the tournament, that when the surfaces are a little bit slower, and there's a bit of hold, how important that length is in forcing them to hit you off your best ball.

"That's what we tried to do as a whole bowling unit, and we did that really well and kept the pressure on."

articles.title: 'Will miss walking out with this rockstar': Travis Head's emotional message for Abhishek Sharma
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The explosive opening partnership between Travis Head and Abhishek Sharma will not be seen in IPL 2027.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The explosive opening partnership between Travis Head and Abhishek Sharma will not be seen in IPL 2027. Head has decided to skip the next season to focus on his international commitments and spend more time with his family, bringing an end to one of the most exciting opening combinations in the tournament.Sunrisers Hyderabad released the Australian batter ahead of the upcoming season. Following the development, Abhishek shared an emotional message for his opening partner on social media on Tuesday.Head also took to social media and posted a series of pictures with Abhishek, remembering their time together at Sunrisers Hyderabad."Will miss walking out with this rockstar," Head wrote.Abhishek responded with a short but heartfelt message for the Australian."Thank you Heady for everything," read his reply.Head and Abhishek formed a destructive opening pair for Sunrisers Hyderabad, putting opposition bowlers under pressure from the start.In 43 appearances for SRH, Head scored 1,351 runs at an average of 32.95 and an impressive strike rate of 176.14. However, his partnership with Abhishek became one of the biggest highlights of his time with the franchise.The duo scored 1,892 runs in 42 innings together at an average of 46.14. They put together six century partnerships and nine stands of at least 50 runs.Only Shikhar Dhawan and David Warner have scored more runs as an opening pair for SRH. However, Head and Abhishek hold a special record. Their scoring rate of 12.46 runs per over is the highest in IPL history among partnerships that have scored at least 1,000 runs.With Head unavailable, SRH will now have to look for a new opening partner for Abhishek at the IPL 2027 auction, scheduled to take place on December 16.Why Travis Head is skipping IPL 2027Head explained that he wanted to focus on his international career while also giving more time to his family. The Australian said leaving SRH was a difficult decision after three memorable seasons with the franchise."After three incredible years with Sunrisers Hyderabad, I want to take a moment to say a heartfelt thank you to everyone who has been part of the journey," Head was quoted in a social media post shared by the franchise."This has been an extremely difficult decision, but with my ongoing international ambitions and the importance of finding a better work-life balance for my family, I feel it's the right one at this stage of my career.""I'm extremely proud of what we've achieved together and will always look back on my time at Sunrisers Hyderabad with great memories and appreciation," the left-handed batter said.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘WE ALL KNEW’: Cameron Bancroft breaks silence on Sandpapergate, admits withholding truth to protect teammates and Cricket Australia
articles.summary: Cameron Bancroft has broken his silence on the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal with a series of explosive revelations, claiming the entire Australian squad
articles.body: Cameron Bancroft has broken his silence on the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal with a series of explosive revelations, claiming the entire Australian squad knew about the ball-tampering plot and admitting that he withheld crucial information during Cricket Australia's (CA) investigation to protect his teammates and the governing body.The former Australia opener, who was caught on television cameras using sandpaper on the ball during the Cape Town Test against South Africa in March 2018, has directly challenged the official version of events that held only he, Steve Smith and David Warner responsible.In an account published in The West Australian, Bancroft wrote: "It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team."He also acknowledged that his account to CA's investigators was incomplete, saying he had deliberately withheld details to avoid implicating others."I did not give a complete and truthful account," Bancroft wrote. "I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others."The admission comes amid renewed scrutiny of the scandal following Usman Khawaja's autobiography, Sabr, in which the former Australia batter claimed the entire team knew about the ball-tampering. Bancroft's account now adds weight to Khawaja's allegations, which have been backed by Warner but strongly disputed by current Australia captain Pat Cummins and other members of the bowling attack.ALSO READ: 'I've got nothing to hide': Darren Lehmann welcomes Cricket Australia's Sandpapergate forumCummins' press conference was the final strawBancroft said Cummins' recent press conference, in which the Australia captain rejected Khawaja's claims and criticised his former teammate for being irresponsible with people's lives and reputations, prompted him to speak publicly."The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference," Bancroft wrote. "It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone."He added: "What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time.""In addition to what Usman already mentioned I have key recollections which affirm what he is saying."Bancroft said he had become the "scapegoat for the entire team", adding that nobody at a meeting after the Cape Town Test had stood up to say they were completely unaware of his use of sandpaper.ALSO READ: Usman Khawaja questions CA's Sandpapergate forum: 'Hard to get the whole truth'Bowlers knew about the ball's condition, Bancroft claimsThe 33-year-old also detailed regular conversations with Australia's fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh, as well as wicketkeeper Tim Paine, about the ball's condition and whether it was reverse-swinging."During that period, I regularly spoke to the bowlers about how the ball was behaving. I had to," he wrote. "I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough."He said the feedback influenced how much sandpaper he used."All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.""Is it going yet? It’s not going yet, it needs more. So I would use the sandpaper more on the ball."Bancroft also alleged that bowling coach David Saker had encouraged him, while media manager Kate Hutchison was the only person in the touring party who openly objected to the practice."I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," he wrote.He recalled Hutchison making it clear that she believed the practice was wrong and walking away from the discussion. "Somebody had spoken up," he wrote. "And I ignored it."ALSO READ: Cricket Australia opens independent forum for players to share 2018 ball-tampering accountsSandpaper plan discussed in dressing roomBancroft said sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa in Port Elizabeth, with Warner proposing that he take responsibility for using it because the cameras were paying close attention to him.He recalled that Saker and then-coach Darren Lehmann were present when the proposal was discussed."I recall people in the room agreeing with the proposal. Saker and Lehmann were certainly present, although I cannot speak for every word shared," he wrote.Bancroft said he felt "uncomfortable and compromised" but went along with the plan, knowing it was wrong. He also claimed Smith "wanted no part" in the discussion and had "distanced himself".He further alleged that after he was caught in Cape Town, team members and staff, including Saker, urged him to lie about what he had used on the ball. Bancroft said his subsequent explanation that he had used yellow tape to collect granules from the pitch was something he now looked back on "with enormous regret"."We were frightened. We were under pressure. We were trying to manage a situation that was rapidly getting away from us," he wrote.Recalling the moment 12th man Peter Handscomb came onto the field to remove the sandpaper, Bancroft said Handscomb told him: "I think it’s time I take that off you now". He added that Lehmann had shouted over the walkie-talkie: "get the f***ing sandpaper off Bangers now"."In my opinion, if he didn’t know he wouldn’t have said that," Bancroft wrote. "Once again. WE ALL KNEW."Bancroft also claimed that ball-tampering practices had become part of the team's routine, saying players had been instructed to push the quarter seam of the ball together after every wicket.He said the scandal had "destroyed" his career. He has not played Test cricket since the 2019 Ashes, despite continuing to score heavily in the Sheffield Shield.CA announced on Wednesday that it would establish an independent forum for players and staff involved in the 2018 South Africa tour to share their accounts. The initiative is not a fresh investigation and will not lead to new sanctions; the board will decide what information can be made public.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: Australia sandpapergate: Cameron Bancroft claims whole team knew of plot in South Africa
articles.summary: Cameron Bancroft claims the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.
articles.body:
Cameron Bancroft has claimed the whole Australia team knew about the 2018 sandpaper plot in explosive revelations that will heap pressure on current captain Pat Cummins.

In a detailed testimony, published by the West Australian, , external batter Bancroft - the player caught with the sandpaper during the Test match against South Africa - has given arguably the most complete account of the events in Cape Town eight years ago.

"In 2018 not the entire truth was told," said Bancroft. "I have never been completely honest about what happened."

For the past two weeks, Australian cricket has been embroiled in a debate over the ball-tampering saga following the publication of Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

Khawaja wrote that the whole Australia team knew of the plot, claims supported by David Warner and Chadd Sayers. Cummins described Khawaja's account as "wrong" and "nonsense".

On the day Cricket Australia announced a forum into the sandpaper episode, Bancroft published his account, explaining he was motivated by the news conference given by Cummins.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," said Bancroft.

"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with - not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa - is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time."

The sandpaper plot - who was there, who said what?

Opener Bancroft was given a nine-month ban for his part in the plot.

Steve Smith was stripped of the Australia captaincy and given a year-long ban, the same suspension given to vice-captain Warner. No other players or coaches were punished.

In his more than 4,000-word piece, Bancroft has claimed:

Sandpaper was first used during the second Test against South Africa – the match before Bancroft was caught

Bancroft had conversations with the Australia seamers – Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether the ball was "swinging enough"

Before the third day of the second Test, the entire playing group and staff had "celebrations" about the effect of the sandpaper

When Bancroft was caught during the third Test, then Australia coach Darren Lehmann told 12th man Peter Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now"

Bancroft found the publication of a joint-statement by the Australia bowlers in 2021 "deeply painful".

Khawaja's autobiography and the subsequent claims made by Warner and seamer Sayers have reopened old wounds related to the sandpaper saga.

Still, those connected have remained true to the accounts they have presented during the intervening eight years.

The most significant denial came from Cummins, who rebuffed Khawaja's account in an extraordinary 68-minute address to the media in Sydney. Lehmann and Starc have also reiterated their denials.

Now, it is the extensive detail provided by Bancroft that could shed a whole new light on the controversy and lead to further questions for Cummins, Lehmann and Cricket Australia.

Cummins is due to lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand on 9 December.

A statement released on behalf of Cummins said: "Whilst we feel for Cam and everything he's been through there's nothing in the statement that hasn't been answered by Pat in his press conference."

A Cricket Australia statement said: "We respect that Cameron Bancroft has told his story, and we will take time to consider his comments.

"We expect that there will be many dimensions to the events of 2018, which is why we have established the forum for individuals to give their version of events.

"We are finalising the terms of reference and will commence the process as soon as possible."

In his account, Bancroft said: "I have spent eight years speaking about accountability, honesty and the lessons I learned from one of Australian cricket's darkest moments.

"However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.

"When I was questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

"I did this to protect Cricket Australia's investigation and not implicate others around me."

Bancroft said his actions were "discussed" and "acknowledged" by the entire playing group at the end of the second day and before the beginning of the third day. He said he was encouraged by Saker, who has since worked as a consultant with England.

The only person within the camp to express unease at the ball-tampering, according to Bancroft, was media manager Kate Hutchison.

"I received wraps and encouragement from members of the playing and coaching staff, especially David Saker," said Bancroft.

"Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening.

"I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

"I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up.

"Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it."

Bancroft identifies Saker as the coach Khawaja claimed encouraged him to work harder on the ball during the third Test in Cape Town. The 33-year-old said he took "feedback" from all the bowlers and wicketkeeper Tim Paine, who took over the captaincy when Smith was sacked.

In Cape Town, Bancroft was confronted by the umpires when TV cameras showed him concealing the sandpaper in his trousers. He claimed Lehmann sent a message to him via Handscomb.

"Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break after I'd been caught and shoved the sandpaper down my pants," wrote Bancroft.

"He said to me: 'I think it's time I take that off you now.' And Pete was doing his job after Boof [Lehmanm] shouted to him on the walkie talkie "get the sandpaper off Bangers [Bancroft] now".

"If he didn't know he wouldn't have said that. And if it wasn't clear enough before, then it was obvious now."

In 2021, Bancroft was playing county cricket with Durham and gave an interview to The Guardian in which he said the bowlers' involvement in the plot was "self-explantory".

In response, Cummins, Starc, Hazlewood and spinner Nathan Lyon released a joint-statement denying any knowledge that ball-tampering had taken place.

"Reading that statement was deeply painful," said Bancroft.

"I had memories of conversations on the field in Port Elizabeth and Newlands, feedback about the ball and shared celebrations that made the statement difficult for me to digest."

Analysis: Potentially the decisive intervention

For almost two weeks, Australian cricket has been at war with itself over the revelations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography.

But there has been an absence of a smoking gun. Without tangible, new, hard evidence, all that was left was claim and counter-claim.

Naturally, the spotlight fell on Pat Cummins because of his role as a bowler in Cape Town and his elevation to Australia captain in the years since.

His performance last week in front of the media, on live television, was extraordinary. For 68 minutes he took all questions and appeared plausible in his answers.

In being so robust in his denial of Khawaja's account - Cummins called it "nonsense" - the skipper also left himself open to the consequences if it was later revealed he was not telling the truth.

Crucially, it was Cummins' press conference that compelled Cameron Bancroft to speak out.

It must be stressed that Bancroft's account is not the open-and-shut evidence that convicts Cummins or anyone else in the dressing room at Newlands in 2018.

But it is certainly the most complete account we have heard from anyone involved, walking step-by-step through the genesis of the plot, the execution and the fallout. Bancroft has named names: Cummins, the other bowlers, Tim Paine, coach Darren Lehmann and assistant coach David Saker. It is, potentially, the decisive intervention that shifts this whole saga in a new direction.

Whether by accident or design, it came on the day Cricket Australia (CA) announced its forum for evidence into the sandpaper controversy. Before Bancroft's account CA's action felt an unsatisfactory halfway house - not an investigation, with no guarantee outcomes will be published.

What now? Will CA go further? How will those implicated by Bancroft respond? How can Cummins lead Australia in the first Test against New Zealand? Could Steve Smith break a silence he has held since the publication of Khawaja's book?

Throughout the past fortnight, there has been a sense that Australian cricket hoped the sandpaper debate would eventually go away. Cummins even said he never wanted to speak about it again.

Instead of fading, the thirst for the truth grows, now fuelled by Bancroft's extraordinary story.

articles.title: Arshdeep Singh makes massive leap in ICC ODI rankings after New Zealand series; Tom Banton climbs to career-best
articles.summary: India pacer Arshdeep Singh has emerged as one of the biggest gainers in the latest ICC Men's Player Rankings, climbing 12 places to reach a career-best
articles.body: India pacer Arshdeep Singh has emerged as one of the biggest gainers in the latest ICC Men's Player Rankings, climbing 12 places to reach a career-best joint 19th position among ODI bowlers following the conclusion of the three-match series against New Zealand. The latest update also saw England's Tom Banton make a significant jump in the batting rankings after his match-winning century against Australia, while several Zimbabwe and Afghanistan players made notable gains in the Test charts.Arshdeep, Matt Henry make big gains in ODI bowling rankingsArshdeep climbed 12 places to share 19th position among ODI bowlers, with Afghanistan spinner Rashid Khan continuing to occupy the top spot. articles.title: 'Made me feel betrayed': Cameron Bancroft blasts Australia captain Pat Cummins over 2018 ball-tampering scandal
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Cameron Bancroft has reignited the 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal by backing Usman Khawaja’s claim that the entire team knew about the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Cameron Bancroft has reignited the 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal by backing Usman Khawaja’s claim that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper against South Africa.He also accused current Australia captain Pat Cummins of betrayal, saying his recent denial of knowing about the incident did not match what Bancroft experienced during the tour.Bancroft, who was banned for nine months after being caught using sandpaper on the ball, admitted that he had not revealed the full truth during Cricket Australia’s initial investigation because he wanted to protect his teammates.In an article for the West Australian, Bancroft said he decided to speak out after Cummins’ 70-minute press conference, where the captain dismissed Khawaja’s claims as “100 per cent wrong” and “irresponsible”.Explaining why he had remained silent for so long, Bancroft said, “The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference. It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.”Bancroft says the entire team knewBancroft directly challenged the earlier version of events, under which only he, Steve Smith and David Warner were held responsible for the scandal. He insisted that other players were also aware of what was happening, including the team's fast bowlers.“It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa,” Bancroft wrote. “It was the whole team.”He further claimed that he regularly discussed the condition of the ball with Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh, as well as wicketkeeper Tim Paine.According to Bancroft, these conversations were about whether the ball was reversing enough and whether more work was needed to make it swing. He also said members of the playing and coaching staff encouraged his efforts, particularly bowling coach David Saker.Cummins's denial questionedBancroft said the support he received made him believe that using sandpaper was accepted as part of the team's collective effort. He also maintained that what he witnessed during the South Africa tour was different from the public version Cummins has presented over the years.His comments come after Cricket Australia announced an independent forum where players can privately share their memories of the scandal without fear of retrospective punishment.Chief executive Todd Greenberg clarified that the move was not a formal reinvestigation, adding that both Cummins and Khawaja were entitled to their own versions of events.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Gurnoor Brar can take Prasidh Krishna's place': Sunil Gavaskar on India's bowling combination for NZ Tests
articles.summary: Former India captain Sunil Gavaskar believes Gurnoor Brar's inclusion in India's squad for the two-Test series against New Zealand is a decision driven by
articles.body: Former India captain Sunil Gavaskar believes Gurnoor Brar's inclusion in India's squad for the two-Test series against New Zealand is a decision driven by conditions, with the former opener suggesting the pacer could get an opportunity if Prasidh Krishna is not fully fit.Brar was drafted into the squad in place of wrist-spinner Kuldeep Yadav, with the team management seemingly looking to add pace and bounce to its bowling options for the challenging conditions in New Zealand. Gavaskar feels the move is also linked to concerns over Krishna's match readiness after his injury layoff.Krishna has not played competitive cricket since suffering an injury during the second ODI against West Indies in Guwahati earlier this year. While his pace and ability to extract bounce offer India a different dimension, Gavaskar believes Brar could step in if the Karnataka pacer is unavailable."Kuldeep’s exclusion was purely condition-based, and Brar can take advantage of the pace and bounce on these pitches as we saw in the ODIs. Also, Prasidh Krishna is coming in without much match practice off his injury, and so he may not be fully ready. Brar has been playing and is match-ready, and is perhaps why he has been included so that he can take Prasidh Krishna’s place," Gavaskar said on Sony Sports.The former India opener also weighed in on India's batting combination, backing Devdutt Padikkal to retain the No.3 position following his impressive performances in the previous Test series against Sri Lanka.Padikkal scored two centuries in two matches against Sri Lanka and also impressed in the warm-up games, strengthening his case for the crucial position. His inclusion comes at the expense of Sai Sudharsan, who had been given opportunities in the format but has yet to establish consistency.Gavaskar believes Padikkal has done enough to make the position his own, while Sudharsan would benefit from spending more time in the longer format."Padikkal has secured the No.3 position with the way he batted in Sri Lanka and even in the warm-up matches. Sai Sudharsan has been up and down in Tests. He needs more experience to solidify himself in Test cricket," Gavaskar said.Padikkal, meanwhile, has credited his conversations with Gavaskar over the years for helping him develop greater clarity about his batting approach and the demands of Test cricket."Obviously, I’ve had a lot of conversations with him over the years in terms of batting and what it takes to really spend long hours out there. Again, it comes back to preparation and understanding what you want to do. As long as you have that clarity in your head about what your plans are and what you want to go out there and do, regardless of the position you’re batting at, it helps a lot. I think those are the conversations I’ve had with him," Padikkal said in an interview with Star Sports.India begin their two-Test series against New Zealand at the Basin Reserve in Wellington on Thursday, November 19. The series carries significant importance for India's World Test Championship campaign, with both matches offering an opportunity to strengthen their position in the race for a place in the final.India have not won a Test in New Zealand since their 10-wicket victory in Hamilton in 2009. With the hosts currently among the leading contenders in the World Test Championship standings, Shubman Gill's side will be looking to overcome that difficult record and keep their qualification hopes on track.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: EXCLUSIVE | Rachin Ravindra: A father's lessons go beyond the boundary
articles.summary: Wellington: It was a busy weekend in the city, with the aroma of coffee roasters filling the streets.
articles.body: Wellington: It was a busy weekend in the city, with the aroma of coffee roasters filling the streets. The overcast morning and chilly winds made it an ideal setting for the perfect pour, but for Ravi Krishnamurthy, it was another day of watching, teaching and talking cricket.Nothing has changed for Ravi, even after his son's meteoric rise on the international stage for New Zealand. The software engineer continues to juggle his corporate job and coaching duties, identifying and nurturing talent at Hutt Hawks. He loves his job, but loves the game of cricket even more. A Level 3-certified coach by New Zealand Cricket, he starts his mornings on the field, and the routine hasn't changed in over a decade."It's the same drill for me: wake up, go to the club, spend time with the boys and then punch in for work. I absolutely love my job, but I also love the game of cricket. Earlier, it used to be early morning sessions with Rachin, and now it's the set of exciting players in the region," says Ravi as he settles down after another hectic morning.The weekend allows him to spare some time after his club duties, and the conversation soon revolves around his son, who has now become an all-format regular for the country. Despite his giant strides in international cricket, for Ravi, Rachin is still the "well-mannered" boy who finds happiness in the sport the household loves. They play and discuss cricket, but ensure that it doesn't become an obsession, even after becoming an important part of their lives."Cricket is important, but at the end of the day, it's not everything. Being happy and content is what matters. That's how we function and think in the house. There are days when we go without discussing cricket. There are times when I even miss watching one of his games. Test cricket is non-negotiable, but limited-overs cricket is at times difficult to keep track of, even for me. But not when it comes to Test cricket," says Ravi.Rachin was recovering from a shoulder injury in the build-up to the Test series against India, but Ravi isn't the nagging father who sought real-time updates. He allowed his son the space to be normal when he was home, with regular household chores taking over and cricket naturally taking a backseat."He is a normal kid at home. He would do the regular vacuuming, clean his cars and be normal, just like everyone else back home. We talk cricket, but not all the time. Even during his injury, I wouldn't ask for real-time updates. I only accompanied him when he wanted a session or a hit. Whenever he wants to train, we go out and seek some sort of private space to get the work done without any distraction," explains Ravi.Apart from his son, Ravi has also overseen the trajectory of several New Zealand cricketers. The likes of Finn Allen, Nathan Smith and Glenn Phillips have all risen through the age-group ranks, where Rachin was the youngest, and shared several memorable moments. Smith, in particular, became very close to the family during his early days, and there was a time when he would even stay at their house when Rachin was travelling for cricket.The bond between Rachin and Smith grew when they played for Wellington and Otago, respectively, at the Under-19 level. Ravi vividly remembers a game in Christchurch when the two were up against each other on a lively green top. Smith caught Ravi's attention, and remarked to his wife that "this boy will play for New Zealand"."That was the same game. I remember Nathan bowling like a dream on a lively surface, and I immediately told my wife that this boy would play for the Black Caps. I was also worried because Rachin was going to face him. Nathan pitched one up, Rachin drove, and the captain immediately opened the field. Aaah, I knew it was done because there was no way Rachin was getting out then, and he didn't. Rachin was younger than them, but playing all his cricket with the older boys helped him improve immensely," recalls Ravi."They are all lovely kids. And Nathan used to stay with us when he played for Wellington, even when Rachin was on the road," adds Ravi.From the IPL to becoming one of the star performers for the Black Caps, Rachin has seen it all during his journey. The boy from Wild Welly made waves in age-group cricket, rose through the ranks and made his first-class debut directly for the A team, well before appearing in the Plunket Shield."It was rare that he played for New Zealand A even before Wellington, but that's how his journey has been. He played two U-19 World Cups, and I knew from the beginning that he would go on to play for the country. But for me, cricket wasn't the obsession; making him a good human being was. What's the point in becoming the best cricketer if you aren't a good person?" asks Ravi before adding, "Cricket will come and go. So will money. But the kind of person you are stays with you forever."Ravi will be immensely proud of the cricketer and person Rachin has become. The all-rounder, who turned 27 on November 18, displays his "good boy" traits even during media interactions, where he makes it a point to thank journalists who wish him luck. It will be a huge moment for the family to see their boy play against India at the Basin Reserve on November 19, but it won't be a surprise if father Ravi squeezes in a quick coaching session before the action gets underway.Cricket is important, but at the end of the day, it's not everything. Being happy and content is what matters. There are days when we go without discussing cricket"I have been doing this for years now, and it's become a habit difficult to let go of," quips Ravi.Finding time for his first love, his job, could pose a hurdle on a working day, but Ravi has juggled both for long enough to have a plan in place.For the father and son, cricket remains a beautiful game that brings immense happiness into their lives. But it's not the be-all and end-all!Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: England cruise to ODI series win over Australia as Ben Duckett scores century and Sonny Baker takes four wickets
articles.summary: England beat Australia by 97 runs in Hobart for 2-1 ODI series win; teams meet in five T20 internationals, starting in Melbourne on Saturday (8.15am UK); 'Sandpapergate' storm rumbles on with Cameron Bancroft backing up Usman Khawaja's claims that every member of team aware of 2018 plot
articles.body:
Harry Brook's side had been skittled for 131 in Perth on Friday en route to slipping 1-0 down in the three-match contest but rallied in Adelaide on Sunday with a 135-run triumph before this convincing result at Ninja Stadium.

Australia were shot out for 231 chasing 329 in the third ODI, with Brook taking the final wicket of tailender Spencer Johnson after seamer Baker claimed 4-45 and spinner Liam Dawson 3-42.

Wednesday's win, England's first over Australia in Hobart, was similar to their success at the weekend: a total above 300 underpinned by a century from an opener - Ben Duckett here after Tom Banton in Adelaide - proving too much for the hosts, whose top order struggled once more when looking to drive.

After Duckett's 133, his seventh ODI ton and first outside England and Pakistan, helped propel his side from 195-5 to 328 all out in 48.3 overs, Australia plummeted to 5-2 and 34-3 in reply - Baker nicking off Mitch Marsh (1) and Josh Inglis (14) with out-swingers.

Australia were eventually dismissed in 46.5 overs with Alex Carey (37) the fifth man to fall, run out after a dismal mix-up with Cameron Green, who later left the field bloodied after being cracked on the helmet by a searing bouncer from Gus Atkinson (1-44) and was replaced by concussion sub Ollie Peake (5).

Just like in Adelaide, the margin of England's victory could have been even greater had they proved sharper in the field, with Baker shelling Matt Renshaw (55) on six running in from deep third and Brook grassing the same player on 54 at wide long-off during the batter's 74 run-partnership with Carey for the fourth wicket.

Banton also spilt Johnson (15) off part-time seamer Brook, two balls before Duckett claimed the winning catch at deep midwicket.

There was one distinct difference from Sunday's game, though, in that England made the maverick call to send Jofra Archer (7 off 7) out to bat at No 6, ahead of Will Jacks (59 off 48), who went on to crack a second successive ODI fifty, this one from 40 deliveries.

The teams will now meet in a five-match T20I series, starting in Melbourne on Saturday (8.15am UK), with England out to do a white-ball double and Australia keen for a victory to bring attention back to on-field matters following the latest 'Sandpapergate' claims.

While the final ODI in Tasmania was ongoing, Cameron Bancroft - the player caught applying sandpaper to the ball in Cape Town eight years ago - wrote an article in the West Australian newspaper backing up Usman Khawaja's allegations that every member of the side back then was aware of the scheme.

Duckett hits hundred before Australia crumble

This was not a great day for Australia. It was not a perfect one for England, either.

The tourists stuttered with the bat once a 74-run opening stand between Banton (44 off 35) and Duckett was snapped in the ninth over as Marsh brilliantly caught the former at mid-off.

Part-time off-spinner Renshaw (3-51) starred with the ball in the absence of injured frontliner Adam Zampa (back spasms), firstly by bowling a charging Joe Root for 12 and having Jordan Cox stumped for the same score and then by ending Duckett's fine knock.

England captain Brook (17) fell cheaply for the third time in the series, after efforts of one and five in Perth and Adelaide respectively, as he skied Cooper Connolly to deep midwicket, while Archer holed out leg-side off Travis Head.

The visitors were tottering at five down for under 200 at the point of Archer's dismissal but Duckett, who was dropped by Carey on 29 and reached three figures from 94 balls, and Jacks combined for a sixth-wicket stand of 56.

Jacks also added 41 with Sam Curran (14) once Duckett fell from a top-edged sweep, before stitching a further 36 runs with the tail.

Atkinson, whose six took England past 300, then continued his dominance of Head (4) by removing the Australia opener for the third time on the trot in this series - Head slashing to Root at slip from the fourth ball of the chase.

When Marsh and Inglis swiftly followed, the home team looked toast and although Renshaw, Carey, Connolly (29) and Jack Edwards (31) - the latter backing up his 4-31 with the ball - gave Australia a flicker of hope, England ran out handsome winners.

Dawson justified his selection ahead of leg-spinner Adil Rashid once again with the wickets of Renshaw caught and bowled, Connolly castled and Edwards pouched on the sweep, while Baker added to his new-ball scalps by removing Peake and Xavier Bartlett (16).

England should be 'proud' but 'work to do' for Australia

England captain Harry Brook , speaking at the presentation:

"It wasn't an ideal start to the series, notoriously we've been a bit slow getting into series.

"But the way we bounced back in Adelaide and the performance we put in today was outstanding. The boys should be really proud.

"The openers [Banton and Duckett] are playing beautifully well together. The height, the left-hand and right-hand combination makes a difference.

"If they keep going nicely, it helps us kick on at the back end of the innings."

Australia skipper captain Mitchell Marsh , speaking at the presentation:

"England outplayed us in the last couple of games and there is lots of room for improvement for our team. We have a bit of work to do.

"I am still excited about this group - a good group of young lads on a journey. The World Cup is 12 months away so bring it on."

Results/schedule for England's Australia tour

ODIs 3.30am UK time, with T20s 8.15am UK time

First T20I: Saturday November 21 (Melbourne)

Second T20I: Tuesday November 24 (Carrara)

Third T20I: Friday November 27 (Brisbane)

Fourth T20I: Sunday November 29 (Sydney)

Fifth T20I: Wednesday December 2 (Canberra)

articles.title: England in Australia: Harry Brook's side win decider for statement series win
articles.summary: England confidently sweep aside Australia in the third one-day international in Hobart to seal a statement series win.
articles.body:
England 328 (48.3 overs): Duckett 133, Jacks 59; Edwards 4-31

Australia 231 (46.5 overs): Renshaw 55; Baker 4-45

England confidently swept aside Australia in the third one-day international in Hobart to seal a statement series win.

At times the series decider felt inconsequential - the latest seismic turn in Australia's sandpaper scandal taking all attention during Australia's chase - but Harry Brook's side won by 97 runs in an important step as they build towards next year's World Cup.

Even when failing to fully take advantage of a fast start, England reached 328 before being bowled out in the penultimate over, with Ben Duckett making a fine 133 from 115 balls.

Duckett's century, after all of his struggles in last winter's Ashes, was his first for England on Australian soil. A 48-ball 59 from Will Jacks ensured his innings was not wasted as Australia's spinners slowed scoring through the middle.

Just as impressive was another exciting effort from England's new-ball pair Gus Atkinson and Sonny Baker.

Atkinson dismissed Travis Head for the third time in a row in the first over - something to be noted before next year's Ashes series. He also hit Cameron Green with a brutal bouncer that forced the all-rounder to retire hurt.

Baker had Australia captain Mitchell Marsh caught at second slip in the second over, soon added the wicket of Josh Inglis and also dismissed Green's concussion replacement Oliver Peake en route to figures of 4-45.

It helped England calmly close out the win and, after being dismissed for 131 in the series opener, their recovery is noteworthy.

Australia, meanwhile, have questions to ponder on and off the field - many of which are unlikely to be answered before a five-match T20 series begins between these sides on Saturday.

On the field, Australia can at least point to the fact key bowlers – most notably under-fire captain Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc and Josh Hazlewood – have been rested for this series as a caveat for their defeat.

On the evidence of this series, England, though inconsistent, look the more settled side.

England had taken strides in ODI cricket this year, beating Sri Lanka (twice) and India, only to be checked by their horror defeats in Pakistan last month. This corrects that course.

Duckett was impressive again but the most significant learning from this series may be the emergence of Baker in partnership with Atkinson.

The 23-year-old Hampshire quick was brought in after defeat in the first ODI and has added real threat with the new ball in his first meeting with Australia.

Bowling has been England's weaker suit in recent ODIs but, given another good start, Liam Dawson was again able to ease through his overs of left-arm spin, bowling Cooper Connolly, having Jack Edwards caught at short fine leg and taking Matt Renshaw caught and bowled with his second ball.

Dropped chances – Baker and Brook put down Renshaw in his 55 and Tom Banton put down a sitter late on – will frustrate, given Brook and the management have spoken of a wish of becoming the best fielding side in the world.

But, after poor run in ODIs which included a failed defence of the World Cup in 2023 and the dismal showing at last year's Champions Trophy, England's 50-over team ends in a much better place than it started.

By having Spencer Johnson caught, Brook even nipped in with the final wicket of the match - his first in ODIs.

Duckett, whose difficult Ashes tour last winter included videos of him apparently drunk circulating on social media, averaged 18.33 across 12 previous innings in Australia before this match. His highest score was 42.

In Hobart, he found a pitch more to his liking – less seam movement, pace or bounce – and capitalised to score a fourth ODI century in a year in which he has switched between feast and famine.

After he and Tom Banton thrashed 73 in the first eight overs, Duckett took responsibility as others fell to Australia's part-time spinners.

Joe Root was bowled by Renshaw for 12, Brook hit Connolly to deep mid-wicket for 17 and Jordan Cox was stumped off Renshaw. Even Jofra Archer was pushed up to number six as a pinch-hitter, only to hole out for a run-a-ball seven off Travis Head.

Throughout it all, Duckett continued. Having driven the quicks early, he slog-swept the spinners until a top edge playing that shot became his downfall in the 39th over.

England's innings fell away slightly but Jacks – once again showing his value – ensured they got a good score.

Duckett's year has been peculiar – England's only Test centurion in their home summer while averaging 26.36 – but this hundred, which follows back-to-back tons on the flat pitches in Pakistan during the recent tri-series, secures his 50-over place going forward once and for all.

England are next in action in this format in January – a timely three-match series against tournament co-hosts South Africa during which they can test their progress in conditions they will face during the World Cup.

articles.title: 'Very hard to let Kuldeep go': Sourav Ganguly opens up on Delhi Capitals' big trade for Rishabh Pant
articles.summary: Delhi Capitals head coach Sourav Ganguly has admitted that parting ways with Kuldeep Yadav was among the toughest decisions the franchise had to make
articles.body: Delhi Capitals head coach Sourav Ganguly has admitted that parting ways with Kuldeep Yadav was among the toughest decisions the franchise had to make ahead of the IPL 2027 season, describing the India spinner as a "very special cricketer".Kuldeep was traded to Lucknow Super Giants in a high-profile deal involving Rishabh Pant, who makes a return to Delhi Capitals at a revised fee of Rs 15 crore. Pant had been signed by LSG for a record Rs 27 crore at the IPL 2025 auction.Explaining the reasoning behind the trade, Ganguly said Delhi were keen to strengthen their batting resources and viewed Pant's return as an important addition to their squad. However, he acknowledged that letting go of a player of Kuldeep's calibre was never going to be an easy call."It was a tough trade because Kuldeep is a very special cricketer. He's been with Delhi Capitals for a long period of time, but in the IPL, with 10 teams, it's always about that one balance factor. And we were looking at a batsman. We got a domestic batsman in Rishabh Pant, who's done well for Delhi. Someone whom I rate very, very highly. But it was very hard to let Kuldeep go, and with Axar and Ashutosh, releasing them was a complete no-no. They are very important part of our squad," Ganguly said on JioStar's 'IPL 2027 Retention Special'.Kuldeep, who had been retained by Delhi at his existing fee of Rs 13.50 crore, will now begin a new chapter with LSG. Pant, meanwhile, returns to the franchise where he spent eight seasons between 2016 and 2024 and also led the side.Ganguly also shed light on the wider considerations that went into Delhi's retention and release decisions, stressing that franchises have to assess several factors rather than follow a fixed formula. According to him, recent performances, squad requirements and the quality of players available at the auction all influence such calls."It's very difficult to pinpoint the exact thought process behind the releases and retentions. It's obviously about performance, who the franchise values and who the franchise thinks is good enough to win cricket matches in the IPL. It is also about what's available at the auction. It's a small auction, so the franchise factors in the performance of the last two years and what it feels is required for the next three years. So, there is no thumb rule that this is right or that is wrong. It's just about faith and belief," he said.Delhi have retained 16 players for the 2027 campaign, with Axar Patel, KL Rahul, Pant and Prithvi Shaw among the prominent Indian names in the group.Their overseas contingent includes David Miller, Kyle Jamieson, Lungi Ngidi and Tristan Stubbs. articles.title: ‘There is no safe space’: Dale Steyn reacts to Cameron Bancroft’s Sandpapergate revelations
articles.summary: Former South Africa fast bowler Dale Steyn has weighed in on the growing controversy surrounding the 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal, dismissing
articles.body: Former South Africa fast bowler Dale Steyn has weighed in on the growing controversy surrounding the 2018 Australian ball-tampering scandal, dismissing the idea that players should be given a “safe space” to share their side of the story without facing criticism.His reaction came after former Australia opener Cameron Bancroft made fresh allegations that the entire team knew about the use of sandpaper during the South Africa tour. Bancroft claimed he was made the “scapegoat” while others escaped responsibility for their involvement.Reacting to the debate on X, Steyn wrote, "“Safe space” Kinda like going to the police, admitting to a crime, then walking away expecting not to be called a criminal for the rest of your life. Good luck with that. There is no safe space."Bancroft claims the entire team knewIn a lengthy article for The West Australian, Bancroft admitted that he had not shared the complete truth during Cricket Australia's investigation in 2018. He claimed that the use of sandpaper began during the second Test in Port Elizabeth and continued into the Cape Town Test.He also alleged that several team members and support staff were aware of the plan.Bancroft recalled wicketkeeper Peter Handscomb taking the sandpaper away from him after he was caught on camera, claiming Handscomb had been instructed to do so by coach Darren Lehmann over a walkie-talkie. He also alleged that David Warner suggested the plan, while Steve Smith did not want to be involved.“It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team,” Bancroft wrote.Bancroft says scandal damaged his careerThe former opener also criticised the public statements made by Australia's bowlers, including Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon, who had previously denied knowing about the sandpaper being brought onto the field.He said Cummins's recent press conference pushed him to finally speak out.“It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone,” he said.Bancroft received a nine-month ban, while Smith and Warner were suspended for 12 months. Claiming the scandal had severely affected his career, he said, "My cricket career has been destroyed and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019."He added that protecting an incomplete version of events had become more damaging than revealing the truth.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.summary: Legendary India batter Sachin Tendulkar joined the cricket fraternity in paying tribute to MS Dhoni after the former India captain brought the curtain
articles.body: Legendary India batter Sachin Tendulkar joined the cricket fraternity in paying tribute to MS Dhoni after the former India captain brought the curtain down on his Indian Premier League playing career following 19 seasons.Chennai Super Kings announced on Tuesday, hours before the IPL 2027 retention deadline, that Dhoni would retire as a player and take up a mentoring role with the franchise. The 45-year-old wicketkeeper-batter's decision was revealed by CSK ahead of the announcement of their retained players for the upcoming auction.Tendulkar took to X to share a heartfelt message, recalling how he first recognised Dhoni's extraordinary power-hitting ability during India's tour of Bangladesh. The Master Blaster also reflected on the memorable moments they shared in the Indian dressing room and congratulated the CSK legend on an illustrious career."I still remember watching MS bat in Bangladesh and telling Sourav that there was something special about his power hitting. You could see he had a rare gift, and what a journey he went on to have."It was a real joy sharing the dressing room with you and being part of some of our most memorable moments in Indian cricket. I always believed you would do something special, and you went on to achieve so much more."You've given Indian cricket your very best, and it's been wonderful to have shared this journey with you. Well played, MS!" Tendulkar wrote.Dhoni's association with the IPL began in 2008, when Chennai Super Kings secured his services for a then-record $1.5 million at the inaugural player auction and appointed him captain. He went on to become the face of the franchise, leading CSK in 244 matches across the IPL and the now-defunct Champions League T20.Under his leadership, Chennai won five IPL titles and two Champions League trophies, taking his tally of silverware with the franchise to seven. Dhoni also accumulated 5,314 runs in the IPL.His association with CSK was briefly interrupted in 2016 and 2017, when the franchise was suspended from the tournament following spot-fixing charges. During those two seasons, he represented Rising Pune SuperGiants.Dhoni last played for Chennai in IPL 2025 and missed the entire 2026 season because of a knee injury. His transition into a mentoring role comes after nearly two decades with the franchise.CSK owner N Srinivasan also acknowledged the former captain's enormous contribution, underlining the special relationship between Dhoni and the franchise."There is no CSK without MS Dhoni," Srinivasan said in a franchise statement. "For nearly two decades, we have walked and grown alongside each other, through triumphs, setbacks and everything in between."Recalling his decision to bring Dhoni to Chennai in 2008, Srinivasan added: "In 2008, I insisted that Dhoni should be part of CSK and it turns out that's the best decision I took. Not because of all his achievements for the franchise, but for the kind of human he is. Dhoni will always be part of our identity. This will always be his home."Dhoni had already brought his international career to a close in 2020, having retired from Test cricket in 2014 and played his final ODI and T20I matches for India in 2019. As captain, he guided India to the 2007 T20 World Cup, the 2011 ODI World Cup and the 2013 Champions Trophy. He also led the team to the No. 1 position in the Test rankings in 2010.Meanwhile, Chennai have made changes to their coaching set-up ahead of IPL 2027, with former India fast bowler Zaheer Khan replacing Stephen Fleming as head coach. Zaheer and Dhoni were teammates in India's 2011 World Cup-winning campaign.While Dhoni's playing days in the IPL have come to an end, his association with Chennai Super Kings will continue in a different capacity, bringing another chapter to a remarkable relationship between the player and the franchise.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates.
